_**User**_

Research task for a desktop "select-to-lookup" dictionary app (Electron, Windows-first, English + Chinese focus). Today's date is Aug 2026 — prefer current information and verify endpoints still exist where you can.

## 1. Free / accessible dictionary data sources
Beyond these already used (Free Dictionary API dictionaryapi.dev, Wiktionary/Wiktextract, unofficial Google Translate endpoints, optional paid DeepL/Oxford/Collins/WordsAPI/Youdao, CC-CEDICT):
Find additional sources usable without payment, ideally without API keys, or with a generous free tier. Consider:
- WordNet / Open English WordNet (and JS/Node packages, offline use)
- Wiktextract / Kaikki.org bulk JSONL dumps (offline-first dictionaries)
- Wikidata / DBnary / BabelNet free tier
- Datamuse API (rhymes, related, means-like, spelled-like — very useful for fuzzy lookup)
- Free Chinese resources: CC-CEDICT, CEDICT variants, HanDeDict, Unihan, Make Me a Hanzi, chinese-xinhua, 汉典 (zdic) availability/ToS, Jun Da frequency lists, HSK lists
- Corpus/example sentence sources: Tatoeba, Reverso (ToS?), Linguee (ToS?), OPUS, Sketch Engine free
- Pronunciation/audio: Wikimedia Commons audio, Forvo (free tier?), open TTS
- Any modern open dictionary APIs that emerged recently

For each: name, endpoint or dump URL, license, offline-capable?, key required?, rate limits, and what data it uniquely adds.

## 2. Etymology sources (this is a priority — current one is "incomplete and brief")
Find the best available etymology data:
- etymonline.com — is there an API? scraping ToS? any mirrors/datasets?
- Wiktionary etymology sections via Wiktextract/Kaikki (structured etymology fields — how good are they?)
- etymwordnet / Etymological Wordnet (Gerard de Melo), EtymDB, IELex, Wiktionary-derived etymology datasets on GitHub/Zenodo
- PIE root databases, Latin/Greek root datasets
- Chinese character etymology: Outlier Linguistics (paid?), 說文解字 Shuowen Jiezi datasets, Wieger, Chinese Etymology (chineseetymology.org / Richard Sears / hanziyuan.net), Make Me a Hanzi (stroke/decomposition), CHISE/IDS decomposition data
Report which give redistributable structured data vs scraping-only.

## 3. Standard query normalization for dictionary lookup
Research how mature dictionary / quick-lookup tools handle the raw selected string before lookup. This is to fix a bug where selecting "word." (trailing period) returns nothing.
Look for actual documented behavior/algorithms in:
- GoldenDict / GoldenDict-ng (its "word processing", punctuation stripping, morphology/Hunspell-based stemming)
- StarDict / Babylon behavior
- macOS Look Up / Dictionary.app behavior
- Youdao / Eudic / Pleco selection handling
- Chrome/Firefox dictionary extensions, Yomichan/Yomitan (deinflection rules), Rikaichamp
- Lemmatization approaches: Hunspell affix stripping, WordNet Morphy, spaCy/lemminflect, simple rule-based suffix stripping
Also research:
- Unicode-aware trimming: which categories to strip (Unicode general categories P* punctuation, S* symbols, Z* separators), handling of internal hyphens, apostrophes (don't, it's), possessive 's, en/em dashes, smart quotes, CJK punctuation 。，、！？「」
- Distinguishing "word" vs "phrase" vs "sentence" for routing to dictionary vs translation (heuristics used in real tools: token count, length thresholds, whitespace, CJK char count)
- Fallback cascade patterns: exact → trimmed → lowercase → lemma → fuzzy/suggest

Give me a concrete recommended normalization algorithm at the end, as ordered steps, including what to strip vs keep, and the fallback cascade. Cite sources with URLs.

---

# Dictionary data, etymology sources, and query normalization

Everything below was verified live on 2026-08-07 unless noted. Sizes and HTTP statuses come from actual requests.

Before the research: **I found the specific cause of your `word.` bug while grounding topic 3.** It's in `src/services/dictionary.ts`:

```307:321:src/services/dictionary.ts
  private isSentence(text: string): boolean {
    // Normalize and coalesce multiple spaces; strip zero-width characters
    const cleanText = text.replace(/[\u200B-\u200D\uFEFF]/g, '').trim();

    // Any text with more than 3 words is a sentence.
    if (cleanText.split(/\s+/).length > 3) {
      return true;
    }
    
    // Check for sentence indicators
    const sentenceIndicators = [
      /[.!?。！？]/,  // Punctuation marks
      /\s+/,     // Any whitespace indicates multiple words
      /[，、；：]/,   // Chinese punctuation
    ];
```

`"word."` matches the first indicator, so it is classified as a sentence and routed to translation rather than dictionary lookup. There is no punctuation stripping anywhere before this check. Separately, `cleanWordForEtymology` uses `/^[^\w]+|[^\w]+$/g`, and JavaScript's `\w` is ASCII-only (`[A-Za-z0-9_]`), so that function destroys accented Latin (`café` → `caf`) and every CJK string (`汉字` → empty). Both are fixed by the algorithm in section 3.

---

## 1. Free / accessible dictionary data sources

### Offline-first bulk data (the highest-value additions)

**Wiktextract raw dump via Kaikki** is the single biggest win available to you. It is the same upstream data as your existing Wiktionary integration but pre-parsed into one JSON object per line, with senses, IPA, inflections, translations, audio links, and etymology all in structured fields.

- Dump: `https://kaikki.org/dictionary/raw-wiktextract-data.jsonl.gz` — verified 200, **2.84 GB** compressed, ~23.1 GB uncompressed ([download page](https://kaikki.org/dictionary/rawdata.html))
- Per-language extracts: `https://kaikki.org/dictionary/downloads/{lang}/{lang}-extract.jsonl.gz` (de, fr, es, ja, zh, etc. — note these are *other Wiktionary editions*, not English glosses)
- Bulk pronunciation audio: 20.4 GB tar of `.ogg` + `.mp3`
- License: CC-BY-SA and GFDL (same as Wiktionary). The wiktextract *tool* is MIT, but the *data* is copyleft — this matters if you ship it inside a proprietary app.
- No key, no rate limit, updated roughly weekly.

The practical approach for an Electron app is to filter the dump down to English + Chinese entries once at build time and ship a SQLite/LMDB index rather than the raw JSONL. [Wiktextract README](https://github.com/tatuylonen/wiktextract)

**Open English WordNet 2024** gives you a proper synset graph: hypernyms, hyponyms, meronyms, antonyms, and short definitions that are cleaner than Wiktionary's.

- `https://en-word.net/static/english-wordnet-2024.xml.gz` — verified 200, 12.9 MB (WN-LMF XML). Also WNDB (10.9 MB, legacy format) and RDF/Turtle (17.8 MB) at [en-word.net/downloads](https://en-word.net/downloads)
- 120,564 synsets, 153,888 entries
- **License: CC-BY 4.0** — permissive, attribution only. This is the most redistribution-friendly serious lexical resource in the list.
- A 2025 edition exists and is reachable through the Python `wn` library as `oewn:2025+`. For Node there is no first-party package; `natural` (MIT, 1.1M weekly downloads) bundles WordNet access, and there's a community `wn-ts-node`.

**Wikidata Lexemes** is worth knowing about mainly because of its license.

- `https://dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidatawiki/entities/latest-lexemes.json.gz` (~566 MB), plus `.ttl.gz` and `.nt.gz`
- SPARQL: `https://query.wikidata.org/sparql`
- **License: CC0** — public domain, no attribution required. Coverage is thinner than Wiktionary but it is the only large multilingual lexical dataset with zero license friction.

**DBnary** is Wiktionary re-modelled in Ontolex RDF across 27 language editions, with a public SPARQL endpoint at `http://kaiko.getalp.org/sparql`. Note a license discrepancy worth checking before you rely on it: the [project page](https://kaiko.getalp.org/about-dbnary/) says CC-BY-SA 3.0 while the [Zenodo records](https://zenodo.org/records/17687058) say CC-BY 4.0. Given Kaikki gives you the same underlying data in a far easier format, DBnary is mostly interesting if you want RDF specifically.

**BabelNet** requires an API key, and the free tier is capped and gated behind a research/personal-use signup at [babelnet.org/guide](https://babelnet.org/guide). Its data is a mosaic of third-party licenses ("all the data of the external resources are released under the terms of the respective owners' licenses"), which makes redistribution genuinely risky for a shipped product. I'd skip it.

### Live APIs, no key

**Datamuse** is the standout recommendation and the best fit for the fuzzy-lookup half of your problem.

- `https://api.datamuse.com/words?...` and `https://api.datamuse.com/sug?s=...` — both verified 200
- No API key, 100,000 requests/day, free for non-commercial use. **Important deadline: from January 1, 2027 an API key will be required for all requests.** Commercial/customer-facing use already requires a negotiated agreement, which is a real constraint if Phevere is ever paid. ([Datamuse API docs](https://www.datamuse.com/api/))
- What it uniquely adds: `ml=` (means-like/synonyms), `sl=` (sounds-like), `sp=` (spelled-like, supports `?` and `*` wildcards), `rel_trg` (trigger words), `rel_jjb`/`rel_jja` (adjectives for a noun and vice versa), plus `md=dpsrf` metadata flags for definitions, parts of speech, syllables, pronunciations, and corpus frequency in a single round trip.
- Relevant to your bug, it is punctuation-tolerant in practice. I tested `?sp=word.&max=3` and got `[{"word":"word","score":8067},{"word":"wordy",...}]`, and `/sug?s=word.` returned `word` first. It's a good "did you mean" backstop.

**Wiktionary REST definitions**: `https://en.wiktionary.org/api/rest_v1/page/definition/{word}` — verified 200 for `word`, returns 30 KB of structured JSON grouped by language. Useful as a lighter-weight live complement to the bulk dump.

**Wikimedia rate limits changed in 2026** and this affects your existing Wiktionary calls. Unidentified requests (no meaningful User-Agent) are now limited to **10 requests/minute**; requests with a compliant User-Agent get **200/minute**. You must send a descriptive `User-Agent` with contact info or you risk 403s and throttling. ([Rate limits](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Wikimedia_APIs/Rate_limits), [User-Agent policy](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Wikimedia_Foundation_User-Agent_Policy))

**Free Dictionary API (dictionaryapi.dev)**, which you already use, has no published limit; maintainer comments in [issue #73](https://github.com/meetDeveloper/freeDictionaryAPI/issues/73) cite ~300 requests per 5 minutes per IP. It's a community-run single point of failure — cache aggressively.

### Chinese resources

| Source | URL | Size (verified) | License | Adds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CC-CEDICT | `https://www.mdbg.net/chinese/export/cedict/cedict_1_0_ts_utf-8_mdbg.txt.gz` | 3.97 MB, 124,766 entries, released 2026-08-05 | CC-BY-SA 4.0 | Trad+simp headwords, pinyin, English glosses |
| Unihan | `https://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/Unihan.zip` | 8.5 MB | Unicode License | Readings (Mandarin/Cantonese/Japanese/Korean), variants, radical-stroke, kDefinition |
| Make Me a Hanzi | `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skishore/makemeahanzi/master/dictionary.txt` | 2.57 MB, ~9,000 chars | LGPL-3.0 (`graphics.txt` derives from Arphic fonts) | Stroke-order SVG paths, IDS decomposition, radical, per-character etymology hints |
| CHISE IDS | `https://github.com/chise/ids` | — | **GPL-2.0** | Most comprehensive IDS coverage |
| cjkvi-ids | `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cjkvi/cjkvi-ids/master/ids.txt` | 2.16 MB | see repo | IDS variant |
| **BabelStone IDS** | `https://www.babelstone.co.uk/CJK/IDS.TXT` | 3.29 MB, 97,058 chars | **Explicit copyright waiver** | Best license of the three IDS sets |
| chinese-xinhua | `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pwxcoo/chinese-xinhua/master/data/word.json` | 27 MB | MIT *(nominal)* | 16,142 chars, 264,434 words, 31,648 idioms, 14,032 xiehouyu |
| Jun Da frequency | [lingua.mtsu.edu](https://lingua.mtsu.edu/chinese-computing/statistics/) | — | academic, cite | Character frequency ranks (data from 2004) |
| SUBTLEX-CH | PLOS ONE paper | — | CC-BY 4.0 | Modern word frequency from film subtitles — better than Jun Da for contemporary usage |

Two license cautions here. **BabelStone's IDS.TXT is the one to prefer** — Andrew West explicitly waives copyright claims ("anyone is free to make use of the IDS data provided in this file for personal or commercial purposes without asking permission or providing attribution"), whereas CHISE is GPL-2.0, which would infect an Electron bundle. And **chinese-xinhua's MIT label is not trustworthy**: the repo README states the data was scraped from various websites and adds 本仓库无任何商业目的！如果有侵权行为将及时删除 ("this repo has no commercial purpose; infringing content will be deleted promptly"). The author cannot MIT-license data they don't own. Treat it as convenient but legally unsettled.

**zdic.net (汉典)** has no public API and no permissive terms. Scraping only, at your own risk.

### Example sentences and corpora

**Tatoeba** is the clear pick for bilingual example sentences.

- Bulk: `https://downloads.tatoeba.org/exports/sentences.tar.bz2` — verified 200, **217 MB**. Also `links.tar.bz2` (translation pairs), `sentences_CC0.tar.bz2`, and `sentences_with_audio.tar.bz2`. Updated every Saturday.
- License: **CC-BY 2.0 FR** by default, with a CC0 subset available separately. Commercial use is allowed; attribution is required and can be satisfied with a link to the sentence.
- API note: `https://api.tatoeba.org/unstable/...` returned 301→404 for me. The working endpoint is `https://tatoeba.org/en/api_v0/search?from=eng&query=word&to=cmn` (verified 200, JSON). Since it's `api_v0` and effectively undocumented, prefer the bulk download for anything production.

**OPUS** offers a live JSON search API at `https://opus.nlpl.eu/opusapi/?corpora=True` (verified 200) over corpora like OpenSubtitles and Europarl. Data is "as-is" with automatic alignment and no manual correction, so quality varies a lot — good for volume, poor for curated examples.

**Reverso and Linguee both prohibit automated access.** Linguee's terms bar forwarding their services to third parties for payment; the popular `linguee-api` package is an unofficial scraping proxy whose own README warns about IP blocking. Neither has an official API. I would not build a shipped feature on either.

### Pronunciation and audio

**Wikimedia Commons is the only genuinely free option.** Wiktionary entries link to `.ogg`/`.mp3` files directly, Kaikki's bulk audio tarball (20.4 GB) gives you them offline, and Lingua Libre feeds thousands of new open-licensed recordings into Commons. Licenses are CC-BY-SA / CC0 per file.

**Forvo has no free tier at all** and its terms are actively hostile to a desktop dictionary. The cheapest plan is $2.00/month for 500 requests/day and prohibits commercial use; audio URLs expire after **2 hours**; and **caching audio is explicitly forbidden**. Every playback also counts as a request. ([pricing](https://api.forvo.com/plans-and-pricing), [terms](https://api.forvo.com/documentation/general-information))

**For TTS, note a license change that matters for Electron.** Piper's original MIT repo (`rhasspy/piper`) was archived read-only in October 2025; active development moved to [`OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl`](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl), which is **GPL-3.0**. If Phevere is or may become closed-source, bundling current Piper is a problem. Your simplest path on Windows-first is the built-in Web Speech API (`speechSynthesis`) in the renderer, backed by SAPI voices, with Commons audio preferred when available.

## 2. Etymology sources

This is where your current "incomplete and brief" complaint has a clean fix, and the answer is not etymonline.

### etymonline: no viable path

There is no public API. `robots.txt` explicitly disallows `/api/` for every user-agent, and the [Terms of Service](https://www.etymonline.com/legal/terms) assert the content is Etymonline's exclusive property protected by copyright. `robots.txt` does `Allow: /word/` for the generic `*` agent, so fetching a word page isn't a robots violation — but that permission is about crawling, not about redistribution, and the ToS govern what you may do with the text.

Your current implementation scrapes `https://www.etymonline.com/word/{word}` with a spoofed Chrome User-Agent (`dictionary.ts:1333-1339`). That is fragile against markup changes, offers no offline story, and is on questionable footing for a distributed app. Existing wrappers (`etymo-js` on npm, `matt-wittmann/etymonline_rest_api`) are all unofficial scrapers with the same exposure; `etymo-js`'s own README tells you to check the ToS yourself.

### Recommended primary: Wiktextract etymology fields

Wiktextract emits two etymology fields per entry, and they are considerably better than a scraped prose blob:

- `etymology_text` — the full etymology section as cleaned human-readable text, with templates expanded and HTML stripped
- `etymology_templates` — a **structured list** of the templates used, each with `name`, `args`, and `expansion`, including nested expansions, with non-etymological templates filtered out

That second field is the important one. Wiktionary etymologies are built from templates like `{{inh|en|enm|word}}` (inherited), `{{bor|en|fr|...}}` (borrowed), `{{der|en|la|...}}` (derived), `{{cog|...}}` (cognate). Because wiktextract preserves the template name and arguments, you can render a real ancestry chain — Modern English ← Middle English ← Old English ← Proto-Germanic ← PIE — with each link typed as inheritance vs. borrowing vs. derivation, rather than dumping a paragraph. That is a genuinely better UI than etymonline gives you, and it's offline.

Caveats: when multiple parts of speech share one etymology section, the same data is copied to each POS entry, so deduplicate. Quality varies by Wiktionary edition — a December 2025 field rename from `etymology_text` to `etymology_texts` caused regressions in some non-English extractors (the Kurdish one lost ~93% of its etymology data, per [issue #1626](https://github.com/tatuylonen/wiktextract/issues/1626)). The English edition, which is what you want, is the best-maintained. ([field docs](https://github.com/tatuylonen/wiktextract))

### Pre-built etymology relation datasets

| Dataset | Access | Scale | License | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **droher/etymology-db** | [GitHub releases](https://github.com/droher/etymology-db) — CSV.gz / Parquet, 140 MB | 4.2M relations, 2.0M terms, 3,300 languages, **31 typed relation types** | Data CC-SA 3.0, code Apache-2.0 | Best structured graph. Last generated **2023-12** — stale, but the extraction code is open so you can regenerate |
| **EtymDB 2.0** | [LREC 2020 paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.392/), GitHub | 1.8M lexemes, 700k+ fine-grained relations, 2,536 languages | CC-BY-SA | Most academically rigorous; distinguishes cognacy from generic origin |
| **Etymological Wordnet** (de Melo) | `http://etym.org/etymwn-20130208.zip` — verified 200, **27.5 MB** | 473k etymological + 538k cognacy relations | CC-BY-SA 3.0 | Still online, but the data is from **2013**. Superseded by the two above |
| **LiLa / LIV** | [CIRCSE/LIV](https://github.com/CIRCSE/LIV) | 7,888 LIV entries, PIE verbal roots → Latin | CC-BY-SA 4.0 | Only the *relations* are published; the LIV text itself is copyrighted by Reichert Verlag |

For PIE roots specifically, there is no comprehensive open database — LIV is copyrighted and only its relational skeleton was cleared for release. In practice Wiktionary's Reconstruction namespace (`Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/*`) is the most complete freely-licensed PIE resource, and it comes along for free in the Kaikki dump.

### Chinese character etymology

The redistributable-vs-scraping split is sharp here:

**Redistributable structured data:**
- **Make Me a Hanzi** — IDS decomposition, radical, stroke-order SVG, and short per-character etymology notes for ~9,000 characters. LGPL-3.0.
- **BabelStone IDS** — 97,058 characters, explicit copyright waiver. Best license for decomposition.
- **Unihan** — `kDefinition`, readings, variants, radical-stroke index. Unicode License.
- **CHISE IDS** — most complete, but GPL-2.0 (avoid for a closed-source bundle).
- **Shuowen Jiezi** — several GitHub transcriptions of the 說文解字 exist with open licenses (e.g. Apache-2.0). The 121 AD text is public domain; only specific modern editions and translations carry rights.

**Not redistributable:**
- **hanziyuan.net / chineseetymology.org (Richard Sears)** — ~96,000 ancient character forms (31,876 oracle bone, 24,223 bronze, 11,109 seal). Free to *view*, no formal open license, no API. Sears has separately released *some* images to Wikimedia Commons under a specific [agreement](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Commons:Ancient_Chinese_characters/Richard_Sears_Agreement) — those Commons files are safe to use; the site's database is not. He asks for donations rather than granting reuse.
- **Outlier Linguistics** — genuinely the best modern scholarly character etymology, but it is a paid Pleco add-on ($29.99 Essentials / $59.99 Expert), closed, with no data access. Not an option.

### Suggested etymology stack for Phevere

Ship Wiktextract `etymology_templates` as the offline primary and render it as a typed ancestry chain. Layer droher/etymology-db on top for cross-language cognate links (regenerating it yourself for freshness). For Chinese, combine Unihan + BabelStone IDS + Make Me a Hanzi. Keep the etymonline scrape only as a manual "open in browser" link, not as a data source — that sidesteps the ToS issue entirely while still giving users access to Harper's excellent prose.

## 3. Query normalization for dictionary lookup

### What mature tools actually do

**GoldenDict-ng** is the most directly applicable reference, and I read its actual implementation rather than the docs. From `src/common/folding.cc`:

```cpp
std::u32string apply( const std::u32string & in, bool preserveWildcards )
{
  // remove diacritics (normalization), white space, punt,
  auto temp = QString::fromStdU32String( in )
                .normalized( QString::NormalizationForm_KD )
                .remove( RX::markSpace )
                .removeIf( [ preserveWildcards ]( const QChar & ch ) -> bool {
                  return ch.isPunct()
                    && !( preserveWildcards && ( ch == '\\' || ch == '?' || ch == '*' || ch == '[' || ch == ']' ) );
                } )
                .toStdU32String();
  // case folding
  ...
}
```

Four ordered stages: **NFKD normalize → remove marks and whitespace → remove punctuation (`QChar::isPunct`, i.e. Unicode general category `P*`) → full case-fold**. Wildcards are preserved when the caller asks. Note it strips `P*` but *not* `S*` (symbols like `©`, `+`, `$`).

A separate, gentler function handles the common trim case:

```cpp
std::u32string trimWhitespaceOrPunct( const std::u32string & in )
{
  // Skip any leading whitespace
  while ( *wordBegin && Folding::isWhitespaceOrPunct( *wordBegin ) ) { ... }
  // Skip any trailing whitespace
  while ( wordSize && Folding::isWhitespaceOrPunct( wordBegin[ wordSize - 1 ] ) ) { ... }
  ...
}
```

That is exactly the operation your app is missing — edge-only trimming that leaves the interior alone.

Crucially, GoldenDict does **not** just fold and search once. It runs a **scored cascade**, keeping several folded variants of the query and ranking results by which variant matched. From the [scoring commit](https://github.com/xiaoyifang/goldendict-ng/compare/xiaoyifang:db72b46...xiaoyifang:6207396), the order is:

```
ScoreExactMatch → ExactNoFullCase → ExactNoDia → ExactNoPunct → ExactNoWs
  → ExactInsideMatch → ExactNoDiaInside → ExactNoPunctInside → ... → PrefixMatch → ScoreWorst
```

The design principle worth stealing: **an exact match always outranks a normalized match.** You never lose `U.S.` or `etc.` to over-eager stripping, because the un-stripped form is tried first and wins if it hits. GoldenDict also layers optional Hunspell morphology on top for stemming and spelling correction, configured by pointing at a directory of `.aff`/`.dic` files. ([features](https://xiaoyifang.github.io/goldendict-ng/), [morphology setup](https://xiaoyifang.github.io/goldendict-ng/manage_sources/))

**Yomitan** (successor to Yomichan) uses a two-phase model: language-specific **text preprocessors** run first (for Chinese, `normalizePinyin` removes spaces and punctuation and lowercases; for Japanese, width normalization, kana conversion, kanji standardization, emphatic-sequence collapsing), then a declarative **deinflection engine** generates base-form candidates. Each rule is `{type: 'suffix'|'prefix'|'wholeWord'|'other', isInflected: RegExp, deinflect: fn, conditionsIn, conditionsOut}`, where the condition bitmasks control which rules may chain. It keeps a `trace` of the rules applied so the UI can show "past tense of X." ([deinflection engine](https://deepwiki.com/yomidevs/yomitan/5.3-deinflection-engine), [text processing](https://deepwiki.com/yomidevs/yomitan/5.2-text-processing))

Yomitan's scanning strategy is also worth copying for CJK, where whitespace gives you nothing. A [C++ reimplementation](https://github.com/Manhhao/hoshidicts) documents it clearly: substrings of the input are tested **from length 16 down to 1**, each preprocessed and deinflected before querying, and results are sorted by matched length first, then by number of preprocessing steps, then deinflection trace length, then frequency. Longest-match-wins with a preference for less transformation.

**macOS Look Up** relies on `NSLinguisticTagger`/`NLTagger`, which tokenizes into words, punctuation, and whitespace as distinct token types (filterable via `.omitPunctuation`/`.omitWhitespace`) and provides a `.lemma` scheme. A well-documented limitation: the lemma scheme is context-dependent and often fails on a bare single word, to the point where the standard workaround is to embed the word in a carrier sentence before tagging. The takeaway is that a full NLP lemmatizer is the wrong tool for isolated selections — dictionary-lookup plus simple rules beats it here.

**10ten Japanese Reader** (formerly Rikaichamp) shows the CJK edge cases you'll hit: it splits around center dots `・` while keeping ruby text intact, handles half-width numerals and full-width forms (`小1`, `８月`, `Ｂ級グルメ`), and suppresses popups for number-only matches. ([release notes](https://github.com/birchill/10ten-ja-reader/releases/tag/v1.27.0))

**Lemmatization options for Node.** `wink-lemmatizer` (MIT) is the pragmatic choice — pure JS, no native build, `noun`/`verb`/`adjective` methods, handles irregulars (`knives`→`knife`, `eaten`→`eat`, `farthest`→`far`). `nodehun` (MIT) gives you real Hunspell `analyze`/`stem` but is a native N-API addon, which means `electron-rebuild` and per-architecture binaries — significant packaging cost for modest gain. `natural` (MIT) bundles WordNet. For reference on the accuracy ceiling, LemmInflect's benchmark over 119,194 inflected words scores LemmInflect 95.6%, spaCy 84.7%, NLTK 52.6% — but it's Python-only, so it's a build-time tool at best.

### Unicode categories: what to strip and what to keep

Modern JavaScript supports Unicode property escapes with the `u` flag, which makes this clean and correct without a table:

- **`\p{P}` (Punctuation)** — strip from edges. Covers ASCII `.`,`!`,`?`,`,`,`;`,`:`,`"`,`'`,`(`,`)`, smart quotes `“”‘’`, en/em dashes `–—`, and CJK punctuation `。，、！？；：「」『』（）《》` in one shot. This alone fixes your bug.
- **`\p{S}` (Symbols)** — strip from edges. Catches `©`, `®`, `+`, `=`, `$`, `¥`, `→`, and emoji, which commonly ride along in a mouse selection.
- **`\p{Z}` (Separators)** — strip from edges. Covers regular space, NBSP `\u00A0`, and CJK ideographic space `\u3000`, which `String.trim()` handles but a naive `[ \t]` regex does not.
- **`\p{M}` (Marks)** — do **not** strip in the main path. Stripping combining marks is a *separate fallback variant* (GoldenDict's `ScoreExactNoDiaMatch` tier), not part of primary normalization, or you'll turn `résumé` into `resume` and return the wrong entry.
- **Zero-width and control characters** — always remove everywhere, not just edges: `\u200B-\u200D`, `\uFEFF`, `\u00AD` (soft hyphen), and C0/C1 controls. Your code already strips the first group in several places; consolidate it.

**Interior characters to preserve.** Hyphens in `well-being` and `state-of-the-art` are part of the headword. Apostrophes in `don't` and `it's` are part of the headword — and note UAX #29 agrees, treating an apostrophe between two letters as non-breaking while treating hyphens as break opportunities. Periods inside `U.S.` and `Ph.D.` are part of the headword. Only the **possessive `'s`** should be stripped, and only as a later fallback step, since `it's` is a legitimate entry while `dog's` is not.

**Normalization form.** Use **NFC** for the primary lookup key. NFKC is tempting because it folds full-width `ｗｏｒｄ` → `word` and ligature `ﬁ` → `fi`, but it also destroys distinctions you may want (superscripts, some CJK compatibility ideographs). The right structure is NFC first, NFKC as a fallback variant. GoldenDict uses NFKD, but it immediately discards the separated marks, which is equivalent to aggressive folding — appropriate for its index, too aggressive for a first attempt.

### Word vs. phrase vs. sentence routing

Your current heuristic fails because it checks punctuation **before** trimming and treats any `.` as a sentence signal. Real tools classify *after* normalization and use token count plus script-aware length:

- Classify only after edge-trimming.
- For scripts with whitespace: count tokens on `\p{Z}+`. 1 token → word. 2–4 tokens → phrase (try dictionary first for multi-word entries like "kick the bucket", fall back to translation). 5+ tokens → sentence, go straight to translation.
- For CJK: whitespace is meaningless. Count CJK characters. 1–4 chars → word or 成语, dictionary. 5–12 → phrase. More → sentence. Presence of `。！？；` **after trimming** (i.e. sentence-internal) is a genuine sentence signal; the same mark at the edge is not.
- A total length guard (~120 chars) short-circuits to translation regardless.

### Recommended algorithm

**Phase A — Sanitize (always, whole string)**

1. Reject null/empty. Hard-cap input length (e.g. 1,000 chars) before any regex work.
2. Remove zero-width and format characters everywhere: `/[\u200B-\u200D\uFEFF\u00AD]/gu`.
3. Remove C0/C1 control characters except tab and newline: `/[\u0000-\u0008\u000B\u000C\u000E-\u001F\u007F-\u009F]/gu`.
4. Collapse all whitespace runs (including `\u3000`) to a single space: `/[\p{Z}\s]+/gu → ' '`.
5. Apply **NFC**: `str.normalize('NFC')`.
6. Trim leading/trailing whitespace.

Call this result `S0`. **Keep it** — it is the exact-match candidate.

**Phase B — Trim edges (this is the bug fix)**

7. Strip leading and trailing punctuation, symbols, and separators, edges only:

```js
const EDGE = /^[\p{P}\p{S}\p{Z}]+|[\p{P}\p{S}\p{Z}]+$/gu;
const S1 = S0.replace(EDGE, '');
```

Do **not** touch the interior. `"word."` → `word`. `“hello,”` → `hello`. `【汉字】` → `汉字`. `well-being` and `don't` and `U.S.` survive intact (the trailing `.` of `U.S.` is trimmed to `U.S`, which is why `S0` must be tried first).

8. If `S1` is empty, the selection was pure punctuation — return no result rather than querying.

**Phase C — Classify and route** (using `S1`, per the heuristics above)

**Phase D — Build the candidate ladder** (generate lazily; stop at first hit)

| # | Candidate | Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `S0` | sanitized, untrimmed — protects `U.S.`, `etc.`, `Ph.D.` |
| 2 | `S1` | edge-trimmed — **fixes `word.`** |
| 3 | `S1.toLocaleLowerCase()` | case fold (skip for CJK) |
| 4 | `S1` minus possessive | `/['’]s$/u → ''` — `dog's` → `dog` |
| 5 | `S1` with `’ ‘ “ ”` → `' ' " "` | smart-quote normalization for interior apostrophes |
| 6 | `S1.normalize('NFKC')` | full-width → ASCII, ligatures |
| 7 | lemma(s) of #3 | `wink-lemmatizer` noun/verb/adjective; try each, dedupe |
| 8 | `S1` minus **all** interior `\p{P}` | last resort — `U.S.` → `US`, `co-operate` → `cooperate` |
| 9 | diacritics-folded #3 | `normalize('NFD').replace(/\p{M}/gu,'')` — deliberately last |

**Phase E — Fallback cascade**

9. Query candidates 1→9 in order against your local index, then remote sources. **Return on first hit**, tagging the result with which candidate matched so the UI can show "showing results for *word*" when it wasn't exact — the same idea as GoldenDict's score tiers.
10. If all miss and the input is a single token, hit Datamuse `/sug?s={S1}` or `/words?sp={S1}` for a did-you-mean list. Both are punctuation-tolerant, so you get a graceful degrade even if normalization missed something.
11. If still nothing, fall through to translation.

**Phase F — CJK longest-match** (when the input is CJK and Phase E missed)

12. Following Yomitan/hoshidicts: take substrings from the start, longest first (cap at ~8 chars for Chinese, which covers 成语), query each, and return the longest match. This handles a user selecting 学习汉字 and getting 学习 rather than nothing.

**Phase G — Per-source hygiene**

13. `encodeURIComponent` every candidate before URL interpolation — you already do this consistently, which is good.
14. Replace `cleanWordForEtymology`'s `[^\w]` with the Phase B `EDGE` regex. As written it silently empties every CJK query and truncates every accented word.
15. Add a descriptive `User-Agent` with contact info to all Wikimedia requests, or you're capped at 10 requests/minute under the 2026 limits.
16. Key the cache on the **candidate that matched**, not the raw selection, so `word`, `word.`, `"word"`, and `Word` all share one cache entry.

**Evidence that steps 1–2 of the ladder are load-bearing.** I tested the failing string against your live upstreams:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `api.dictionaryapi.dev/api/v2/entries/en/word.` | **404** |
| `api.dictionaryapi.dev/api/v2/entries/en/word` | 200 |
| `en.wiktionary.org/api/rest_v1/page/definition/word.` | **404** |
| `en.wiktionary.org/api/rest_v1/page/definition/word` | 200 |
| `en.wiktionary.org/w/api.php?action=opensearch&search=word.` | 200 → `["word","worden","Word"]` |
| `api.datamuse.com/sug?s=word.` | 200 → `word` first |

Neither of your two primary sources tolerates the trailing period, so the fix must happen client-side. But Wiktionary's `opensearch` and Datamuse's `/sug` both recover gracefully, which makes them ideal for step 10.
